problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.statement:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.

An Anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
commonMistakes: Sorting strings which adds O(K log K) overhead
Delimiter collisions in frequency string without separators
hints: Words are anagrams if their character counts are identical.
Generate a 26-element character count tuple as the hash map key.
Group words by key in a Hash Map.
Sort each group to ensure deterministic testing.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

parameterDefinitions.name: k
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of top elements to return

constraints: k is in range [1, number of unique elements]
The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Top K Frequent Elements testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using standard full sort O(N log N) instead of bucket sort O(N)
Off-by-one in frequency buckets count up to N
hints: First count frequencies with a Hash Map in O(N).
Can you avoid sorting by using the maximum frequency N as bucket indices?
Iterate backwards through frequency buckets from N down to 0.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

The product of any prefix or suffix of `nums` is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(N)` time and without using the division operation.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Product of Array Except Self testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using division (prohibited by prompt)
Failing on multiple zeros
hints: Product except self at i is (prefix product before i) * (suffix product after i).
Compute prefix products in a first pass from left to right.
Accumulate suffix products on the fly in a second pass from right to left in O(1) extra space.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1500 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.statement:
Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(N)` time.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Longest Consecutive Sequence testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Checking every element instead of only sequence starts (where num - 1 is not in set)
Not handling empty array
hints: Insert all numbers into a Hash Set for O(1) lookups.
Only begin counting a sequence if num - 1 does not exist in the set (i.e. num is the start of a sequence).
This ensures each number is visited at most twice, maintaining O(N) linear time.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return `true` if `nums` has a good subarray or `false` otherwise.

A good subarray is defined as:
- length of at least 2
- the sum of elements is a multiple of `k`.

examples.explanation: [2, 4] sums to 6 which is a multiple of 6.
Edge/boundary case for Continuous Subarray Sum testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Overwriting first seen index in map when same remainder appears
Not requiring length >= 2
hints: If prefixSum[j] % k === prefixSum[i] % k, then the elements between i and j sum to a multiple of k.
Store the EARLIEST index at which each remainder was seen in a Hash Map.
Check that j - i >= 2.

hints: Use modulo arithmetic: if two prefix sums have identical remainder modulo k, their difference is divisible by k.

problems.title: Isomorphic Strings
problems.statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, determine if they are isomorphic.

Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`.

All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. No two characters may map to the same character, but a character may map to itself.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII character.

examples.explanation: o cannot map to both a and r

commonMistakes: Checking only one-way mapping instead of bijection
hints: A character mapping must be bijective (one-to-one and onto).
Use two maps (s->t and t->s) or record last seen positions.

problems.title: Ransom Note
problems.statement:
Given two strings `ransomNote` and `magazine`, return `true` if `ransomNote` can be constructed by using the letters from `magazine` and `false` otherwise.

Each letter in `magazine` can only be used once in `ransomNote`.
constraints: ransomNote and magazine consist of lowercase English letters.
commonMistakes: Reusing the same magazine character multiple times
hints: Count the frequency of each letter in magazine.
Iterate through ransomNote, decrementing count for each char.
If count becomes negative, magazine lacks sufficient characters.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.statement:
Write an algorithm to determine if a number `n` is happy.

A happy number is a number defined by the following process:
- Starting with any positive integer, replace the number by the sum of the squares of its digits.
- Repeat the process until the number equals 1, or it loops endlessly in a cycle which does not include 1.
- Those numbers for which this process ends in 1 are happy.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Happy Number testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Infinite loop without cycle detection
hints: Simulate the digit sum operation.
Use a Hash Set or Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm to detect repeating cycle states.

hints: Store the last seen index of each element in a Hash Map.

problems.title: 4Sum II
problems.statement:
Given four integer arrays `nums1`, `nums2`, `nums3`, and `nums4` all of length `n`, return the number of tuples `(i, j, k, l)` such that:
- `0 <= i, j, k, l < n`
- `nums1[i] + nums2[j] + nums3[k] + nums4[l] == 0`

Given a string `s` which consists of lowercase or uppercase letters, return the length of the longest palindrome that can be built with those letters.

hints: Even counts of characters can always be placed symmetrically on both sides.
Odd counts can have count - 1 letters placed symmetrically.
At most one odd character can be placed in the center.

problems.title: Majority Element II

Given an integer array of size `n`, find all elements that appear more than `floor(n / 3)` times.

Not verifying candidates in second pass
hints: How many elements can appear more than floor(n / 3) times? At most 2.
Use Boyer-Moore Voting algorithm extended to 2 candidates and 2 counters.
Perform a second verification pass to confirm frequencies.
